raw:
You leave the loan register closed and the green album in its locked cupboard. The blue box on the table is a different case.

Nell lays its acquisition record beside the blank sheet. “This tells you why we can call it trust property,” she says, indicating the transfer schedule. “The programmes themselves can tell you dates and titles. Keep those sources separate.”

The first paper-wrapped bundle contains weekly programmes, still in their original order. Together, you record it as a group: printed programmes; dates taken from the covers; softened edges and creases, with the wrapper torn at one corner; transferred with the former cinema’s business archive; owned by the trust.

Nell has you note that the date range comes from the programmes themselves, rather than treating the acquisition paperwork as proof of when they were issued. She checks the completed entry, then slides the next bundle within reach.

“That’s the method,” she says. “Work steadily. If the order seems meaningful, preserve it. If something doesn’t match the records, stop and mark it for me.”

She takes the folder back to the office, leaving the archive workroom quiet around you.

You begin on the next bundle, keeping its wrapping and sequence intact as you describe what is there. The locked cupboard remains at the far end of the room, separate from the trust-owned material on the shelves.
